column1: # Famous games library (G1). One row per game of famous_games.pgn, same order. Descriptions are Palaya's own words.

column8: description
The 16th game of the fourth match between Alexander McDonnell and Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais, played in London in 1834.
A casual game played in London in 1851, the year of the first international chess tournament; known ever since as the Immortal Game.
A casual game played in Berlin in 1852 by Adolf Anderssen and Jean Dufresne; known as the Evergreen Game.
Played at the First American Chess Congress in New York in 1857, which Paul Morphy won.

column5: Duke Karl of Brunswick and Count Isouard
column8: Played in 1858 in a box at the Paris opera, against two noblemen consulting together; known as the Opera Game.
The ninth game of the 1858 match in Paris between Paul Morphy and Adolf Anderssen, which Morphy won.
Played at the London tournament of 1862, the first international tournament of the future world champion Wilhelm Steinitz.
Played in Vienna in 1872 by Carl Hamppe and Philipp Meitner; known as the Immortal Draw.
Played at the London tournament of 1883, which Johannes Zukertort won ahead of Wilhelm Steinitz.
The first game of the 1886 match between Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort, the first match for the title of world champion.
The 20th and last game of the 1886 match, played in New Orleans; Steinitz won the match and became the first official world champion.
Played in Amsterdam in 1889 by the 20-year-old Emanuel Lasker, five years before he became world champion.
Played at the Dresden tournament of 1892, which Siegbert Tarrasch won; the opening trap in it is named after him.
Game 19 of the 1894 title match, played in Montreal; with this win Emanuel Lasker took the world championship from Wilhelm Steinitz.
Played at the great Hastings tournament of 1895; Curt von Bardeleben left the hall instead of resigning and lost on time.
Played at the four-player tournament in Saint Petersburg in 1895-96, which the world champion Emanuel Lasker won.
Played at Cambridge Springs in 1904, eight years after their game in Saint Petersburg, against the reigning world champion.
Played at Cambridge Springs in 1904 between the world champion Emanuel Lasker and the young William Napier.
Played in Lodz in 1907 between Georg Rotlewi and Akiba Rubinstein; known as Rubinstein's Immortal.
The tenth and last game of the 1910 title match; Lasker's win levelled the match and he kept the world championship.
A casual game played in Vienna in 1910 between Richard Réti and Savielly Tartakower; one of the best-known short games.
Played in Hamburg in 1910; the chess game in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey follows its final moves.
Played at San Sebastián in 1911, the tournament José Raúl Capablanca won on his first appearance among Europe's leading masters.
Played at Breslau in 1912; known as the Gold Coins Game from the story that spectators showered the board with gold coins.
A casual game played in London in 1912, famous for a king hunt that takes the black king across the whole board.
Played in the final stage of the Saint Petersburg tournament of 1914, which Lasker won half a point ahead of Capablanca.
Game 10 of the 1921 title match in Havana, in which José Raúl Capablanca won the world championship from Emanuel Lasker.
Played at Hastings in 1922 between Efim Bogoljubov and Alexander Alekhine, five years before Alekhine became world champion.
Played in Copenhagen in 1923 between Friedrich Sämisch and Aron Nimzowitsch; known as the Immortal Zugzwang Game.
Played at the Baden-Baden tournament of 1925, which Alexander Alekhine won.
Game 34, the last of the 1927 title match in Buenos Aires, with which Alexander Alekhine won the world championship from Capablanca.
Played in Warsaw by the young Miguel Najdorf, on a date that sources give as 1928, 1929 or 1930; known as the Polish Immortal.
Played at Hastings in 1930-31; a win by Mir Sultan Khan over the former world champion José Raúl Capablanca.
Played by Esteban Canal of Peru against an amateur in a simultaneous exhibition in Budapest in 1934; known as the Peruvian Immortal.
Game 26 of the 1935 title match, played in Zandvoort; Max Euwe won the match and the world championship. Known as the Pearl of Zandvoort.
Played in Rotterdam during the AVRO tournament of 1938, between the future champion Mikhail Botvinnik and the former champion Capablanca.
Played in the 1943 Uruguayan Championship between B. Molinari and Luis Roux Cabral; known as the Uruguayan Immortal.
Game 23 of the 1951 title match in Moscow; Botvinnik's win levelled the match, which ended drawn so that he kept his title.
Game 14 of the 1954 title match in Moscow between Mikhail Botvinnik and Vasily Smyslov.
Played in New York in 1956 by the 13-year-old Bobby Fischer against Donald Byrne; known as the Game of the Century.
The first game of the 1960 title match in Moscow, which the 23-year-old Mikhail Tal won to become world champion.
Game 6 of the 1960 title match in Moscow, won by the challenger Mikhail Tal with the black pieces.
Game 21, the last of the 1961 return match in Moscow, in which Mikhail Botvinnik regained the world championship from Mikhail Tal.
Game 19 of the 1963 title match in Moscow, which Tigran Petrosian won to become world champion.
Game 10 of the 1966 title match in Moscow, won by the world champion Tigran Petrosian, who kept his title.
Game 19 of the 1969 title match in Moscow, which Boris Spassky won to become world champion.
Played in the 1960 Soviet championship in Leningrad; a version of its final position appears in the film From Russia with Love.
A correspondence game between two Swedish players, 1964-65; its final position was printed on a Swedish postage stamp in 1985.
Played at the 1970 match in Belgrade between the Soviet Union and the Rest of the World, on first board.
Game 6 of the 1972 title match in Reykjavík, which Bobby Fischer won to become world champion.
Game 13 of the 1972 title match in Reykjavík, a long game won by Bobby Fischer with the black pieces.
Played in Kirovabad in 1973; Eduard Gufeld called this win his Mona Lisa.
Game 32, the last of the 1978 title match in Baguio; Anatoly Karpov's sixth win kept him world champion.
Game 32 of the 1984-85 title match in Moscow, Garry Kasparov's first win of a match that was later stopped without a result.
Game 16 of the 1985 title match in Moscow, won by the challenger Garry Kasparov with the black pieces.
Game 24, the last of the 1985 title match in Moscow; Kasparov's win made him, at 22, the youngest world champion up to then.
Game 16 of the 1986 title match, played in Leningrad, between Garry Kasparov and Anatoly Karpov.
Game 22 of the 1986 title match in Leningrad; with this win Garry Kasparov reached the 12 points he needed to keep his title.
Game 20 of the 1990 title match, the fifth match between Garry Kasparov and Anatoly Karpov, played in Lyon.
Game 24, the last of the 1987 title match in Seville; Garry Kasparov needed a win to keep his title, and won.
Played in Brussels in 1991 in the Candidates quarter-final match between Vassily Ivanchuk and Artur Yusupov.
Played at the Hoogovens tournament in Wijk aan Zee in 1999 between Garry Kasparov and Veselin Topalov; known as Kasparov's Immortal.
Played over the internet in 1999: Garry Kasparov against moves chosen by a vote of thousands of players from many countries.
Played at Dortmund in 2003, when Teimour Radjabov was 16, against Viswanathan Anand.
Game 2 of the 2006 reunification match in Elista between Veselin Topalov and Vladimir Kramnik.
The fourth rapid game of the 2006 tiebreak in Elista; Vladimir Kramnik's win reunified the world championship title.
Game 6 of the 2008 title match in Bonn, which Viswanathan Anand won.
Game 12, the last of the 2010 title match in Sofia; Viswanathan Anand's win decided the match.
Game 8 of the 2012 title match in Moscow; at 17 moves, one of the shortest decisive games in world championship history.
Played in round 4 of the Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee in 2013; known as Anand's Immortal.
Game 5 of the 2013 title match in Chennai, Magnus Carlsen's first win on the way to the world championship.
Game 6 of the 2013 title match in Chennai, Magnus Carlsen's second win of the match.
Game 9 of the 2013 title match in Chennai, Magnus Carlsen's third win of the match.
Game 11 of the 2014 title match in Sochi; Magnus Carlsen's win kept his world championship.
Game 10 of the 2016 title match in New York, Magnus Carlsen's first win of the match, which levelled the score.
The fourth rapid game of the 2016 tiebreak in New York, played on Magnus Carlsen's birthday; his win kept the title.
The third rapid game of the 2018 tiebreak in London, after twelve drawn games; Magnus Carlsen won all three rapid games and kept his title.
Game 6 of the 2021 title match in Dubai; at 136 moves, the longest game ever played in a world championship match.
Game 8 of the 2021 title match in Dubai, Magnus Carlsen's second win of the match.
Game 4 of the 2023 title match in Astana, Ding Liren's first win of the match.
Game 12 of the 2023 title match in Astana, a win by Ding Liren that levelled the match.
The fourth rapid game of the 2023 tiebreak in Astana; Ding Liren's win made him the first world champion from China.
The first game of the 2024 title match in Singapore, won by the defending champion Ding Liren with the black pieces.
Game 3 of the 2024 title match in Singapore, Gukesh Dommaraju's first win of the match.
Game 11 of the 2024 title match in Singapore, which put Gukesh Dommaraju ahead in the match for the first time.
Game 14, the last of the 2024 title match in Singapore; the win made the 18-year-old Gukesh Dommaraju the youngest undisputed world champion.
The first game of the 1996 match in Philadelphia, the first game a computer won against a reigning world champion under tournament conditions.
The second game of the 1996 match in Philadelphia, which Garry Kasparov won to level the score; he went on to win the match.
The sixth and last game of the 1996 match in Philadelphia; Garry Kasparov's win gave him the match by 4 points to 2.
The first game of the 1997 rematch in New York, won by Garry Kasparov.
The sixth and last game of the 1997 rematch in New York; Deep Blue's win made it the first computer to beat a world champion in a match.
